- Cards 5–6 are `loading=lazy`. Their requests start at Low priority 89–236 ms after the 4 eager ones, and CDP showed no priority boost.
- After loading they run the 300 ms opacity ramp (SafeImage.tsx:140-142, 155; fade=true in the DOM).
- The live bundle Products-OJ9kO6p4.js still has `eager:s<4` (Products.tsx:286). Nothing after 7c7190b changed SafeImage, ProductCard or Products image loading. No srcset, edge rule or wrapper handles it.

**What is wrong in the finding**
1. **The LCP claim fails.** The LCP element is a row-1 eager card, now a 2 KB image (…fcbb8e3f9.webp?w=480). Cards 5–6 are the same size and can never be the LCP. Measured from the first image request to LCP (medians):
   - live: 357 ms
   - offscreen images held back (IntersectionObserver gate): 360 ms
   - first 6 eager plus the gate: 350 ms
   - first 6 eager alone: 450 ms, slightly worse, because two more High-priority images share the link

   The 10 offscreen Low images do not delay LCP measurably, so "LCP gain about 0.1 s" is wrong.
2. **"Bigger once the catalogue exceeds 26" is wrong for image bytes.** On 4G, Chrome's native lazy-load margin is 1250 px. 800 + 1250 = 2050 px reaches 8 rows, so 16 images, whatever the catalogue size; on a 3G-class connection the margin is 2500 px. Only the cost of rendering up to 50 cards grows, and that was not measured.
3. **Making the first 6 eager does nothing by itself.** First screen fully visible, median ms after the first image request:
   - live: 1632
   - first 6 eager alone: 1641
   - gate alone: 1323
   - first 6 eager plus gate: 816
4. **On category listings it mostly does not apply.** The grid in ProductGrid.tsx:46 also uses `i < 4`, but it starts at top 243. There cards 5–6 begin at 743, so only about 57 px of them show on an 800 px screen.

**Caveat on the model:** DevTools throttling shares bandwidth equally between requests and ignores HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 priorities. Over real Cloudflare HTTP/2 with Chrome's priority ordering, cards 5–6 are the first Low requests and would go first. So the share caused by offscreen bandwidth (about 0.3 s) is an upper bound. The 300 ms fade and the 90–240 ms later start do not depend on the network.

Severity: low to medium. LCP is unchanged; the bottom row of the first screen appears about 0.5–0.8 s after the rest.
gains: The gain is not in LCP: about 0 ms, and at most −0.1 s on average. Live medians from the first image request were 416, 422 and 317 ms; the trace shows link sharing cost the LCP image 36 ms at most. The gain is the third row (cards 5-6) and the first screen finishing sooner on a Slow-4G phone. With live per-image server TTFBs that is about −0.3 s (model: 2160 → 1830-1880 ms), mostly from dropping the 300 ms fade and starting cards 5-6 at High priority 100-270 ms earlier. When the variants are edge-cached it is up to −1.1 s (1813 → 669 ms), because 16 images stop sharing a 1.6 Mbps link. Bytes before scroll drop from 261 KB to 97 KB (6 images) or 124 KB (correct 300 px margin on the scroller). That only holds if the observer is rooted at #main-scroll-container; with the default root, scrolling gets worse because rows start loading only once they are on screen.

**LCP: about 0 ms.** Medians of 357, 360 and 350 ms after the first image request for live, gate, and 6-eager plus gate. The 6-eager change alone made it about 90 ms worse.

**First screen fully painted on a phone** (360×800×3, CPU ×4, Slow-4G, cold cache, 5 runs per arm), medians after the first image request:
- live: 1632 ms (range 1083–2191)
- 6-eager plus the IntersectionObserver gate: 816 ms (range 718–1988), about 0.8 s sooner
- gate alone: 1323 ms, about 0.3 s sooner
- 6-eager alone: 1641 ms, no gain

Counted from LCP, the bottom row of the screen finishes 1275 ms after LCP today and 513 ms with both changes.

Of the roughly 0.8 s:
- 300 ms is the fade, a fixed cost.
- About 150 ms comes from the lazy start after layout.
- About 0.3 s is bandwidth shared with the 10 offscreen images. That last part is an upper bound, because real HTTP/2 priority ordering would shrink it.

**Bytes before any scroll:** 261 KB down to 95 KB (−166 KB). That does not grow with the catalogue, because native lazy loading already stops at 16 images on 4G.

confirmed.title: Light-theme main photo loses its aspect and downloads the 1080 copy where the 800 copy covers it
confirmed.routes: /product/:slug on the light theme (the default 'system' theme on a light-mode phone), for products that open on the primary photo
confirmed.cause: When the light theme swaps the primary for light_image, the gallery sets `width: null, height: null` (Product.tsx:2233). productGallerySizes(mediaAspect(activeMedia)) at line 4084 then falls back to the frame-width PRODUCT_GALLERY_SIZES (calc(100vw - 58px) = 302 px), which asks for 906 device px and picks ?w=1080. The square photo is actually drawn object-contain at about 255 CSS px (765 device px), which ?w=800 covers.
confirmed.measured: Phone trace imgs: the main reports sizes = the frame preset, currentSrc ?w=1080 and a drawn box of 255×255 content. curl with Accept: image/avif: - pla-basic light image fd6146…: ?w=1080 44,274 B vs ?w=800 30,612 B (−31 %). - p1s light image d8b974…: 30,500 vs 21,576 B (−29 %). - h2d LCP light image ?w=1080: 38.7 KB.
confirmed.fix: Expose the light image's stored width and height (its product_images row or R2 metadata) in the detail and card JSON and keep them in the swapped gallery entry, so the aspect-aware sizes apply. Expected: −9 to −14 KB on the LCP photo (about 50–70 ms on Slow-4G).
reasons: The finding is real, but it is rated wrongly. It overstates the cost on the phone size it measured and misses the phones where it costs the most. Code, checked at 7c7190b: - src/pages/Product.tsx:2233 swaps the primary for light_image and sets `width: null, height: null`. - Product.tsx:4084 calls `productGallerySizes(mediaAspect(activeMedia))`. With no aspect, packages/contracts/src/imageSizes.ts:78 returns the frame preset PRODUCT_GALLERY_SIZES (`calc(100vw - 58px)` on a phone). - `naturalWidth` is also null (Product.tsx:4085), so the srcset uses plain rung descriptors (`?w=1280 1280w`, `?w=1600 1600w`). - Nothing else handles this. worker/lib/socialPreview.ts:418 turns the document preload off whenever light_image is set, and no other srcset, sizes or lazy wrapper applies. - The light image is a bare string column (migration 0138, MainImagesPair.tsx), so no stored size exists. The proposed fix of exposing the light file's width and height is the right one. Scope: 25 of the 27 public products from /api/products have a light_image, all 1254×1254 squares. So this hits almost every product page for a light-mode or "system" visitor. Live, real Chromium, light vs dark, same page (/product/bambu-lab-pla-basic-filament, h2d, p1s). Main currentSrc: - 360@3, 384@2.81, 393@2.75, 412@2.625: light picks ?w=1080, dark picks ?w=800. The drawn photo is about 255–295 CSS px (771–774 device px on the three wider screens), so 800 covers it. - 412@3.5 and 430@3: light picks **?w=1280**, dark picks ?w=1080. The frame is 354–372 CSS px, so it needs 1116–1239 device px and crosses the 1080 rung. - 390@3, 360@2, 375@2: same copy in both themes, so no cost. curl with Accept: avif: - For these 1254 px originals, ?w=1280 returns the full original WebP: 102,016 B, the original's etag, no Vary. - ?w=1080 is an AVIF of 44,274 B. Equivalent pairs: p1s 65,762 vs 30,500 B; h2d 77,176 vs 37,677 B. - So on big phones the overshoot costs 2.2–2.3× the bytes. - This compounds with a server fault: imageVariants.ts:77-79 intends the top rung to be a small re-encode, but live serves the original. A/B on the live page, light theme, cold cache, Slow-4G 150 ms + CPU×4. The request was rewritten in Playwright to simulate the fix: - 360@3, 1080 vs 800 (4 pairs): image 45.3 vs 31.6 KB. Median transfer 533 vs 510 ms. Median LCP 4624 vs 4616 ms, within noise. The finding's claimed 50–70 ms does not show up. - 430@3, 1280 vs 1080 (4 pairs): image 103.0 vs 45.3 KB. Median transfer 1190 vs 602 ms. Median LCP 6000 vs 4992 ms. Paired LCP deltas were −292, −308 and −1200 ms, plus one outlier pair at 8888 ms. Verdict: not "low −9 to −14 KB, 50–70 ms" across the board. - Negligible on 360–412 phones at DPR ≤3. - Medium on large DPR-3 and 3.5 phones (iPhone Plus/Pro Max, Pixel Pro class, 430+ CSS px or DPR 3.5), where it costs 0.3–1 s of LCP. The finding missed this. - Fix as proposed. Optionally also make ?w=1280 of a ≤1280 original return the AVIF re-encode, which caps the overshoot everywhere. Evidence is in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-lightsizes/: pick-pla.log, pick-h2d-p1s.log, curl.log, ab-360.log, ab-430b.log.

The finding is real, but the rating is wrong. The cost it names (1080 instead of 800, −9 to −14 KB) is the small part. The large cost is on wide phones, and the finding does not cover them.

Code (checked at 7c7190b):
- src/pages/Product.tsx:2233 swaps the primary for light_image with `width: null, height: null`.
- Line 4084 `productGallerySizes(mediaAspect(activeMedia))` therefore returns PRODUCT_GALLERY_SIZES (packages/contracts/src/imageSizes.ts:55, `calc(100vw - 58px)` on a phone).
- `naturalWidth` is null too, so `variantSrcSet` does not stop at the stored width: it lists `?w=1280 1280w, ?w=1600 1600w`.
- The light originals are square. Their WebP headers read 1254×1254, the same as the dark primaries. So the photo is drawn object-contain at min(78vw,340)−26 CSS px, not at the frame width.
- Nothing else repairs this. There is no later srcset, no edge rule and no wrapper.
- The document preload cannot help either. worker/lib/socialPreview.ts:418 skips the preload whenever light_image differs from the primary, so these pages have no preload at all. That is a separate cause.

I checked which file Chromium picks with a local copy of the gallery box (zero live requests; scratchpad/perf/skeptic-lightsizes-x/pick.log). Light now / with the aspect / dark:

| Phone (CSS px @ DPR) | Light now | Light with aspect | Dark |
|---|---|---|---|
| 360@3, 375@3, 384@2.81, 393@2.75, 412@2.625 | 1080 | 800 | 800 |
| 390@3, 414@3 | 1080 | 1080 | 1080 (no gain) |
| 360@2, 375@2 | 640 | 640 | 640 (no gain) |
| 428@3, 430@3, 412@3.5, 360@4 | **1280** | 1080 | 1080 |

The 1280 row is the expensive one. For a 1254 px original, `?w=1280` is answered with the ORIGINAL WebP: no X-Variant-Source header and the original's exact length. It falls back at worker/routes/uploads.ts:1072–1093 instead of returning an AVIF copy.

Live sizes, curl with an AVIF Accept header, six light images:
- 800 → 21.6–42.8 KB
- 1080 → 30.5–62.1 KB (AVIF)
- 1280 → 65.8–146.8 KB (WebP original)

So 1080→800 saves 9–19 KB (−29 to −31 %), and 1280→1080 saves 35–85 KB (−51 to −66 %).

Live A/B in Chromium: bambu-lab-pla-basic-filament, 430×800 @3, light colour scheme, CPU ×4, Slow-4G (1.6 Mbps, 150 ms), cold, 2 runs each. In variant B the `?w=1280` request was rewritten to `?w=1080` (log: scratchpad/perf/skeptic-lightsizes-x/ab430.log). Real currentSrc in both = w=1280 with the frame sizes, so the finding's mechanism is confirmed.

| Variant | Bytes | Image download | LCP |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (now) | 102,016 B | 1275 / 1213 ms | 6612 / 5076 ms |
| B (aspect-aware) | 44,274 B | 507 / 604 ms | 4704 / 4512 ms |

Image download is about −0.69 s, and LCP minus image start is about −0.65 s.

At 360@3 the parallel skeptic's 8-run A/B on the same product (scratchpad/perf/skeptic-lightsizes/ab-360.log) found no visible effect: image 533 vs 510 ms, LCP 4624 vs 4616 ms, inside the noise.

Scope:
- 25 of the 26 product JSONs checked carry light_image, but only pages that open on the primary photo are hit.
- The audited route /product/esun-pla-plus is NOT hit: its main image is a selection photo (152564b1…, 1000×444). The light file appears only as a 64 px thumbnail there.
- The dark theme is fine, because the primary's width and height are known.

Verdict: real but mis-rated.
- Low (≈0.05–0.1 s on Slow-4G) for typical Android widths.
- Zero on 390 and 414 iPhones.
- Medium (≈0.6–0.7 s of LCP on Slow-4G, ~60–85 KB) on 428/430@3 iPhones and DPR ≥3.5 Androids.

The proposed fix is right: carry the light file's stored width and height, so both the aspect-aware sizes and the srcset cap apply. Making the 1280 rung of a 1254 px original return an AVIF copy (instead of the 2.3× larger original WebP) would shrink the worst case for every picture, not only this one.
gains:
360–412 CSS px phones at DPR 2.6–3 (most Android): −8.9 to −13.7 KB on the LCP photo (−29 to −31%). That is about 40–65 ms in theory on Slow-4G, but not measurable: the paired median LCP was 4624 vs 4616 ms.

≥430 CSS px at DPR 3 or 412 at DPR 3.5 (iPhone Plus/Pro Max, Pixel Pro): −35 to −58 KB (102,016 B original WebP down to a 44,274 B AVIF). Measured image transfer drops 1190 → 602 ms median, and LCP improves about 0.3–1.0 s (median 6000 → 4992 ms).

390/393 at DPR 3 and DPR 2 phones: 0.

Applies to 25 of 27 product pages in light mode.

These are the savings on the LCP photo if the light file keeps its width and height (aspect-aware sizes):

- **360–412 px Android phones at DPR 2.6–3 (and 375@3):** the 1080 copy becomes the 800 copy, −9 to −19 KB (−29 to −31 %, measured live with curl).
  - That is about 45–95 ms of transfer on Slow-4G and about 10–15 ms on a typical 10 Mbps 4G.
  - The 8-run live A/B at 360@3 showed no LCP change beyond noise (4624 vs 4616 ms).
- **390@3 and 414@3 iPhones:** no change (both versions pick 1080).
- **428/430@3 iPhones, 412@3.5 and 360@4 phones:** the 1280 rung, which is the original WebP of 65–147 KB, becomes the 1080 AVIF copy of 30–62 KB, saving 35–85 KB.
  - My live A/B at 430@3, Slow-4G, CPU ×4 (pla-basic, 2 runs each): image download 1244 → 555 ms median, LCP 5844 → 4608 ms mean.
  - The like-for-like LCP gain is about 0.65 s on Slow-4G; on a real 10 Mbps 4G it is about 50–100 ms.

The finding's estimate (−9 to −14 KB, 50–70 ms) covers only the smallest-phone case.

confirmed.title: Printer detail JSON ships the spec table twice (≈33 KB gz) before the page can render; neither copy is visible on first paint
confirmed.cause:
The detail answer, preloaded by the document and awaited before the page renders (Product.tsx:2143), carries:
- spec_groups in three languages, rendered only inside the collapsed «المواصفات» Section (Product.tsx:4390, defaultOpen false);
- the legacy `specifications` alias (products.ts:2192, legacySpecs), which the page renders only when spec_groups is empty (Product.tsx:4392), so for these products it is never used.

Both download in the critical window, alongside ~330 KB of product JS on the same link.
confirmed.measured: bambu-lab-h2d /api/products/<slug>: 237,416 B raw / 35.7 KB on the wire. spec_groups is 151,551 B raw / 25.0 KB gz; specifications 31,682 B raw / 8.3 KB gz. bambu-lab-p1s: 160 KB raw / 28.8 KB on the wire (spec_groups 98 KB raw). Trace runs/h2d.json: the API (37.2 KB) loads 439 → 2157 ms while the product JS loads until 3602 ms; about 33 KB gz of avoidable bytes ≈ 165 ms of Slow-4G bandwidth in that window.
confirmed.fix: Omit `specifications` when spec_groups is non-empty. Serve spec_groups on demand when the section opens (a small cached GET), or at least only in the page language. Expected: about −33 KB on printer pages' critical download (≈0.1–0.17 s earlier render on Slow-4G).
reasons:
This is a real cause of slow display, but a small one, and the finding overstates two of its numbers.

Code checks out:
- worker/routes/products.ts:2192 always adds `specifications: legacySpecs(doc)` to the public answer, through publicShape at :2196.
- Product.tsx:4390 puts spec_groups inside a Section that starts closed (Section at :805 has defaultOpen=false and renders nothing until clicked).
- Product.tsx:4392 uses legacySpecs only when spec_groups is empty.
- No other first-paint code reads either field. The only other frontend reader of `specifications` is a type in src/lib/api.ts.
- The document preloads /api/products/:slug (worker/lib/socialPreview.ts:875, worker/index.ts:967). It is not handled anywhere else: there is no lazy split, no language filter and no entry in docs/PERFORMANCE_LOG.md or docs/DECISIONS.md.

Live re-measurement (anonymous curl, 2026-10-16):
- bambu-lab-h2d detail is 237,416 B raw and 34,448 B on the wire. The wire encoding is brotli, not gzip; Node brotli at quality 4 reproduces it at 34,169 B.
- What matters is how much the brotli answer shrinks, not each field compressed on its own. Removing only `specifications` saves 3,897 B on H2D, 4,212 on H2C and 2,420 on P1S. That is not the 8.3 KB claimed: the field repeats the Arabic labels and values already in spec_groups, and brotli back-references them.
- Trimming spec_groups to one language (and dropping `specifications`) saves 14.9 / 16.1 / 9.8 KB.
- Removing both fields from the first answer saves 25.5 / 27.4 / 17.2 KB, not about 33 KB.
- Only 3 of the 27 live products are affected (all printers). Every other product carries at most 4.5 KB of spec bytes, and at most 0.55 KB of `specifications`.
- JSON.parse of the full answer takes 0.53 ms against 0.07 ms without the spec fields, so parsing time is negligible.

Browser A/B on the phone profile (360×800 DPR 3, CPU ×4, Slow-4G, 7 interleaved runs per arm). Both arms served the same live H2D document. Arm B added a 28.7 KB on-the-wire fetch preload in the same slot as the detail preload:
- Median FCP went from 3316 to 3520 ms (+204), mean from 3390 to 3518 (+128).
- The last critical script (vendor-motion) finished +218 ms later at the median.
- Mean LCP did not change (4403 vs 4398); run-to-run noise in image loading swamps it.

So these bytes do compete for bandwidth in the critical window. The detail data is not itself the gate: it lands about 1 s before the last JS.

Rating and fix:
- "Low" severity is right.
- The first proposed fix, omitting `specifications`, is worth only about 4 KB, roughly 20 ms, which is negligible on its own.
- The real gain comes from moving spec_groups off the critical answer. One option is to fetch it after first paint, at idle or when the section opens; fetching only on open costs a round trip of about 0.6 s on Slow-4G when the user taps the section. Sending only the page's language gives about 60% of that gain.
- Note: the live asset hashes changed after the audit ran, but the API sizes are byte-identical.

The cause is real, but the finding overstates the bytes, and its first proposed fix does almost nothing.

Re-checked against the code:
- **Live code has moved on.** The live site now runs a newer head (≤0d8ed43): the live Product-BRPeh8Sn.js has the lazy ProductKnowledgeTabs. The cause is still there:
  - worker/routes/products.ts:2170/2194 still adds `specifications: legacySpecs(doc)` to every public detail.
  - spec_groups still carries all three languages, 478 rows for H2D.
- **The page waits for the detail.** It shows the skeleton until the detail arrives (src/pages/Product.tsx:2210 `if (loading || !product)`). The detail is preloaded by the document (`<link rel=preload as=fetch href=/api/products/bambu-lab-h2d>`).
- **Neither copy is visible at first.** The specs Section (Product.tsx:4555) is closed by default, and src/components/product/Section.tsx:41 renders its children only when open.
- **The new knowledge tabs do not replace it yet.** GET /api/products/bambu-lab-h2d/knowledge and /bambu-lab-p1s/knowledge both return empty specs (157 B), so the page still draws the old Section from spec_groups.
- **Listings are not affected.** /api/products?limit=5 cards have no spec fields.

What the finding gets wrong, from my live measurements with curl:
- **The served size is smaller than claimed.** Chrome gets zstd: 35,574–35,652 B, cf HIT. Brotli is 34,448 B, gzip 39,496 B.
- **The finding measured the wrong way.** It compressed each field on its own with gzip. Measured inside the real response with the edge's compressors (zstd-3 gives 35,624 and brotli-4 gives 34,169, matching live), removing both copies saves 26.4 KB zstd for H2D, not 33 KB.
  - The legacy `specifications` copy alone costs only 3.8 KB zstd, not 8.3 KB, because the compressor already removes most of the duplicate. So "omit `specifications`" saves about 18 ms even on Slow-4G, which is too small to matter.
  - The fix worth making is to fetch spec_groups only when the section opens, or at least in one language. One language plus no alias saves 14.3 KB.
  - H2C: 28.5 KB for both copies. P1S: 18.2 KB.
- **The detail is not the last thing the page waits for.** In the earlier trace it finished at 2157 ms while the JS finished at 3602 ms. Its only cost is the download speed it takes from the JS on the same slow link.

Browser A/B test:
- **Setup.** I recorded the live page once and replayed it locally, byte for byte, through Chrome with the same phone throttling as the audit (Slow-4G at 1.6 Mbps and 150 ms RTT, CPU ×4, 360×800). Only the detail body changed between runs: 20 runs with the full body against 20 with spec_groups and the alias removed.
- **Results** (mean ± standard error, median in brackets):

| Moment | Full body (ms) | Specs removed (ms) | Change (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Product title painted | 3620 | 3507 | −113 ± 58 (median −205) |
| Largest image painted | 4391 | 4214 | −178 ± 67 |
| First paint | 3115 | 2973 | −142 ± 56 |

This matches the simple estimate: 26 KB at 1.6 Mbps is about 125 ms. JSON parsing and building the hidden row elements add only a little.

**Verdict:** real and correctly rated low, but the bytes are about 26 KB, not 33 KB. The primary fix should be deferring spec_groups, not dropping the alias. The gain is about 0.1–0.2 s only on a very slow link. On a normal 4G phone (10 Mbps or more) it is about 20 ms.

Scratch files are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-specdup-k/: ab-h2d.json, ab-h2d-2.json and the data/ folder. The scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-specdup-k-scripts/ (replay.mjs, marg.cjs).
gains:
Printer pages only (H2D, H2C, P1S). On Slow-4G at 1.6 Mbps (about 205 KB/s):
- Moving spec_groups and specifications off the preloaded detail answer saves 25.5 / 27.4 / 17.2 KB brotli. That is about 85–135 ms earlier FCP by bandwidth arithmetic; the A/B gave +128 ms mean and +204 ms median for 28.7 KB, and showed no measurable LCP change.
- Sending spec_groups in the page language only saves 14.9 / 16.1 / 9.8 KB, about 50–80 ms.
- Omitting `specifications` alone saves 3.9 / 4.2 / 2.4 KB, about 12–20 ms, which is negligible.
- On real 4G (5–10 Mbps) the full fix is worth about 20–40 ms.
- The other 24 products gain under 5 KB.

Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-specdup-scripts/sizes.cjs and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-specdup-scripts/ab2.mjs. Data: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-specdup/all/

Phone lab profile (Slow-4G, CPU ×4), bambu-lab-h2d, local replay of the live page, 20 runs per arm:
- **Fetch spec_groups and the alias only when «المواصفات» opens.** The detail goes from 35.7 KB to 9.3 KB on the wire (zstd). Product title paints 113 ± 58 ms earlier (median 205 ms); largest image 178 ± 67 ms earlier; first paint 142 ± 56 ms earlier.
- **One language plus no alias:** −14.3 KB, about 70 ms.
- **Dropping only `specifications`** (the finding's first fix): −3.8 KB, about 18 ms. That is negligible and below the test's noise.
- **Other printers:** P1S −18.2 KB (about 85 ms); H2C −28.5 KB (about 135 ms).
- **On a normal 4G phone** (10 Mbps or more), the whole 26 KB is about 20 ms or less.

refuted.title: Product page fetches every gallery thumbnail and colour swatch with the lead picture, including dozens off-screen in the horizontal strip
reasons:
The off-screen requests are real, but removing them does not make the page appear sooner, so the cost is negligible. Some details of how the finding explains it are also wrong.

Code (perf/live 7c7190b): the thumbnail strip is at src/pages/Product.tsx:4111 (SafeImage `sizes="64px"` at :4133). The swatches are at :3326, :3384 and :3514 (40px) and :3584 (36px). All of them use SafeImage's default `loading="lazy"` (src/components/ui/SafeImage.tsx).

What I re-measured live on /product/bambu-lab-pla-basic-filament (Playwright at 360x800 DPR 3, dark, CPU x4, CDP Slow-4G 150 ms / 1.6 Mbps, cold). Script and logs are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-thumbstrip/ (cap.mjs, ab3.mjs, ab4.mjs, cap1.log, ab3.log, ab4.log):

1. The image requests at load are as the finding says: 45 in total, made of the lead picture, 5 visible thumbnails and 39 off-screen (9 thumbnails and 30 swatches).
   - The off-screen bodies total about 71 KB: 28.7 KB for thumbnails 6-14 at ?w=320 and about 42.6 KB for the swatches at ?w=160, measured with curl.
   - The finding's 104 KB counts roughly 1 KB of uncompressed headers per request. The sandbox reaches the site over HTTP/1.1 through the proxy. The real site serves HTTP/2 (with 103 Early Hints) and offers h3 (alt-svc), where those headers shrink to almost nothing.
2. Some of the finding's description is wrong:
   - Chrome's margin does NOT cover the whole strip. Only 14 of 31 thumbnails load: 5 visible plus 9 within about 2 strip-widths. The other 17 wait for a scroll.
   - The swatches are not in the horizontal scroller. They are a vertical list at 868-1912 px, below the 800 px fold. Chrome fetches them because its lazy-load distance for the whole screen (1250 px or more) reaches that far.
   - Each colour list is drawn twice (a hidden 0x0 copy), but both copies use the same addresses, so no extra bytes are downloaded.
3. The off-screen requests start at the same moment as the lead picture, about 70 ms after it (lead at 3.7-4.7 s, after first paint at about 3.5 s). So they cannot delay first paint: median first paint was 3,554 / 3,518 / 3,496 ms across the three versions in batch 1.
4. Test of the finding's realistic fix: keep the lead picture and the 5 visible thumbnails, cancel the 39 off-screen ones. Two batches of 6 and 7 cold runs, alternating with the normal page. Because the lead picture's start time swings by about ±500 ms from run to run, the fair measure is LCP minus the moment the lead picture is requested:

| Batch | Normal | Fix | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 805 ms | 747 ms | −58 ms |
| 2 | 738 ms | 838 ms | +100 ms |

   - Median LCP moved by −144 ms in batch 1 and +212 ms in batch 2.
   - Single runs within one version range from 4.41 to 6.22 s, so these differences are noise and the fix has no measurable effect.
5. Test of the finding's other fix: hold every thumbnail and swatch until the lead picture has finished.
   - The lead picture downloaded in 481 ms instead of 613 ms, and the LCP-minus-request measure fell from 738 to 652 ms (−86 ms). The finding's own "LCP-only" version, which also drops the visible thumbnails, gave −195 ms (805 → 610 ms).
   - The cost: the 5 visible thumbnails finished about 490 ms later (median 1,392 vs 906 ms after the lead picture's request).
   - The test setup also exaggerates the competition. The CDP throttle splits the bandwidth evenly between up to 6 HTTP/1.1 connections. On a real phone over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, Chrome marks the lead picture as high priority (`fetchpriority=high`) and the thumbnails and swatches as low priority, so Cloudflare sends the lead picture first. The real gain is below these upper bounds of 0.1-0.2 s.
6. The real reason this route is slow lies elsewhere and is outside this finding. The PLA Basic page's document preloads no image: its links name only CSS, the font, /api/products/…, and modules. That matches the deliberate suppression for galleries tied to colour choices (PERFORMANCE_LOG 2026-10-04 follow-up). So the lead picture is only requested at 3.7-4.7 s, once the JavaScript, the API answer and the first render are done. That is what makes LCP about 4.5-5 s, not the thumbnails.

Verdict: the bytes are real, but their effect on display time is within noise and negligible. The proposed fix for the off-screen requests shows no measurable LCP gain. Holding everything until the lead loads buys under 0.1 s in a pessimistic test and makes the visible thumbnails about 0.5 s late.

I re-measured this on the live site and re-read the code. The extra requests are real, but they do not make the page appear later in any way I could measure.

1) The code is as the finding describes. The strip (/home/user/levonis-perf/src/pages/Product.tsx:4110-4136) and the swatches (3320, 3378, 3508, 3578) are lazy SafeImage with fetchPriority auto. The lead picture is eager with fetchPriority high (Product.tsx about 4072-4085, /home/user/levonis-perf/src/components/ui/SafeImage.tsx). Each SafeImage's onLoad only sets its own state, so it does not re-render the page.

2) Some facts in the finding are wrong. Only 14 of the 31 thumbnails load at start (5 visible, 9 off-screen); the other 17 wait for a scroll. The 30 colour swatches are not in a horizontal scroller. They are a vertical list just below the fold (top 868 to 1912 px at 360x800). Chrome loads them because of its normal lazy-load distance (1250 px on 4G). They are the same pictures as the thumbnails at w=160 instead of w=320.

3) The browser request order protects the lead picture. CDP shows the lead requested at High about 140 ms before the others (4359 vs 4498-4508 ms in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-thumbstrip-c/full1.log). The off-screen images go out at Low; only the visible ones move to High. All variants are edge cache HITs, so the lead's response is not waiting while the small images fill the link.

4) My A/B test (ab.mjs, results in ab-slow4g.log in the same folder): phone 360x800 at DPR 3, CPU x4, Slow-4G, cold image cache, 5 interleaved runs per arm. Static JS was served locally to cut noise. In the "fix" arm, the 39 off-screen requests were held unanswered, as if they had no src.
- LCP median: 2480 ms normal vs 2492 ms fix, so no gain.
- Time from lead request to paint: 705 vs 613 ms.
- Lead picture download: 610 vs 516 ms, about −94 ms.
- Time from lead image arrival to paint: 84 vs 80 ms, so no main-thread cost.
- The 5 visible thumbnails were not delayed (770 vs 1004 ms, noise).
- The finding's own A/B agrees: −130 ms against ±250 ms of noise.

5) The ~90 ms is an upper bound from the test setup. DevTools throttling splits bandwidth evenly across all open requests and ignores priority. In this sandbox Chromium also runs HTTP/1.1 through the interception proxy (protocol http/1.1, proxy CA). The live site serves h2 (curl gets h2 straight through to Cloudflare) and advertises h3, where Cloudflare sends High before Low. On a real phone the lead picture should lose roughly 0-50 ms.

Result: about 100 KB of extra data on colour-rich products, but not a cause of slow display. A cheap tidy-up for data use only: give the swatches the thumbnails' w=320 copy, or hold them until the lead picture's onLoad. Do not expect a faster LCP from it.

refuted.title: The product grid renders every card at once, so 16 images (10 below the fold) download together with the LCP image
reasons:
The code reading is correct, but the mechanism and the cost are not. Products.tsx:275-286 and src/components/listing/ProductGrid.tsx:39-46 do render every card. Only cards i<4 are eager. In SafeImage.tsx:150-152 that means loading=eager with fetchpriority=high; every other card is loading=lazy with fetchpriority=auto. Chrome's 1250 px lazy-load distance applies: on a 360x800 phone, rows up to top=1963 px load and the row at 2231 px does not. So /products requests 16 images, 10 of them below the first screen (167 KB of 277 KB). What the finding gets wrong is the claim that those 10 share the link with the LCP image.

1) The finding misreads its own trace. CDP's requestWillBeSent is the time the renderer asks for a file, not the time bytes start moving. In this lab, Chromium goes through the agent proxy, which intercepts TLS and serves only http/1.1 (response.protocol = http/1.1 on every request, issuer "CCR agent-proxy interception CA"). Chrome's limit of 6 sockets per host then queues the below-fold requests. I ran the same phone profile on the live site: 360x800, DPR 3, CPU x4, Slow-4G 150 ms / 1.6 Mbps, cold context. In 10 baseline runs of /products and 4 of /categories/printing-materials/fdm-materials, no below-fold image response began before the LCP image had finished (0 overlaps in 14 runs). The listing requests 14 images, not 16, and 8 of them are below the first screen.

2) A/B test of the proposed fix. Arm B holds every below-first-screen /files/ image request until all first-screen images have finished, which is what "assign src only after LCP" would do.
- /products, n=10 per arm: LCP median 3710 → 3624 ms. Most of that gap was noise before the images: the median image request start already differed by 62 ms. The part the fix can claim is LCP minus the LCP image's request start: 672 → 638 ms. The LCP image's download went 606 → 572 ms. That is about -35 ms.
- fdm listing, n=4 per arm: LCP median 5456 → 5364 ms, mean 5637 → 5604 ms. The LCP image's download got longer, 453 → 529 ms, so this is within noise.
- Run-to-run spread inside arm A alone was 3436–4188 ms.

3) Real phones would not see the 0.4–0.7 s either. They talk h2 or h3 to Cloudflare (alt-svc: h3=":443"). CDP shows the below-fold lazy images at initialPriority Low and never raised. The first-screen images are High: the 4 eager ones from fetchpriority=high, and row 3 raised after layout. Cloudflare schedules response bytes by priority (h2 priorities, RFC 9218 on h3). The 0.4–0.7 s figure only holds if bandwidth is split equally among all streams. That is how DevTools throttling behaves, not how a prioritizing server does. The leftover risk is one case: the LCP image is slow at the origin (once I saw a 614 ms TTFB on an R2 read) and low-priority bytes fill the window in the meantime. That costs at most about one congestion window, roughly 0.1 s on Slow-4G.

4) The proposed fixes would not help:
- fetchpriority=low on the other cards changes nothing, because those images are already Low.
- "Render about 8, append the rest after first paint" would still start those images before the LCP image arrives.
- Windowing would only save some of the grid's render work. The grid commits in 70–125 ms long tasks at CPU x4, so that is about 30–60 ms.

Where /products LCP actually goes: /api/products ends at about 2.0–2.2 s, all 26 cards are in the DOM at 2.8–3.1 s, the first images are requested at about 3.0 s, and then the first screen's 6 images (about 110 KB) share the link for about 0.6 s. Those 6 are needed for the first screen, and they are not what this finding is about.

Evidence: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-grid/ab.mjs, products-ab.json, products-ab2.json, fdm-ab.json, first.json, lt.mjs.

The code is as the finding describes. The mechanism it claims is not what happens. Removing every below-fold image does not move LCP.

Code (live head c9265b0, the same as 7c7190b for these files; only the card height changed, 262 to 280 px):
- src/pages/Products.tsx:285 and src/components/listing/ProductGrid.tsx:43 render all cards with eager={i < 4}.
- SafeImage.tsx:155-157 turns that into loading="eager" plus fetchPriority="high" for the first 4. Every other card gets loading="lazy" and fetchPriority="auto".
- So the finding's alternative fix is already in place. The first two rows already have fetchpriority=high. The other images already start at Low priority, so adding fetchpriority=low to them would change nothing.

What I measured on the live site (Playwright Chromium, 360x800, DPR 3, CPU x4, Slow-4G 150 ms / 1.6 Mbit/s, cold context; scripts and JSON in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-grid2/):

1. Request timeline on /products (products-slow4g.json):
   - 16 images are requested at about 3.43-3.53 s.
   - The 4 High images get their response at 3691-3779 ms and finish by 4022-4079 ms.
   - The 10 below-fold images (Low) get no response bytes until 4256 ms or later, after the High images have finished.
   - The finding's evidence counts "requested at" as "downloading". It is not: Chrome holds the Low requests back.

2. Test A against C, where C blocks (aborts) every image outside the first screen. This is the best any windowing fix could do.
   - /products, 5 runs each: median LCP is 3664 ms for A and 3728 ms for C. The LCP image download takes 610 ms against 629 ms.
   - fdm-materials, 4 runs each: median LCP is 5820 ms against 5604 ms. Almost all of that gap comes from the image request starting earlier (5235 against 4959 ms), not from contention. LCP minus image start is 730 against 675 ms, about 55 ms.
   - A previous run in skeptic-grid/products-ab.json, which held the images back instead of blocking them, shows the same: LCP image download 435-671 ms in A against 349-701 ms with the images held.

3. Test F against T: the same API answer served in both arms, but T keeps only 8 products, as in the proposed fix.
   - The time from the API answer to the first image request is 1143 ms with 26 cards and 1113 ms with 8.
   - The final long task is about 120-185 ms with 26 cards and about 50-85 ms with 8.
   - Median LCP is 3736 against 3580 ms. Individual runs vary by about ±250 ms, so this is noise.

Why the LCP image still takes about 0.6 s:
- 150 ms RTT, plus Worker/R2 server time, plus sharing the link with the other 3 High first-screen images (about 74 KB). The proposed fix keeps those images.
- LCP is the first equal-size card image to paint, not the last one.

What actually holds /products back:
- The grid cannot request its images until about 3.0 s, even when the API answer is ready at 1.8 s. The roughly 1.1 s in between is JS and boot work.
- On fdm-materials the products API itself only starts at about 4.3-4.8 s.
- Both of these are separate findings.

Caveats:
- The sandbox proxy forces Chromium onto HTTP/1.1, and its README says to report rather than work around this. So I could not measure HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, which a real phone uses.
- On h2/h3, all 16 images go out at once. The edge serves them by Chrome's priorities (High before Low), but bytes are sent in whatever order they become ready. The leftover risk is Low bytes sent while the High responses are still waiting on R2.
- The finding's 0.4-0.7 s figure only holds if the link is shared equally with no prioritisation. My own fair-share calculation with the real sizes gives about 0.8 s, and that is a worst case, not what was measured.
- Lighthouse's simulated LCP (Lantern, pessimistic graph) may still count these images, so the PSI score could move slightly even though real display time does not. I did not measure this.
- The bytes are real: 127-167 KB of below-fold images download for a user who never scrolls. That costs data, not display time.

refuted.title: Small shell reads compete with the route chunks: settings fetched twice on the home page, community access on every page, /api/bundles never edge-cached
reasons:
The facts in the finding are correct. The claim that these reads slow display is not, and the measurements show no effect.

1) Facts confirmed. The /api/home answer on the live site carries a `settings` object with the same keys as /api/settings/public, 11,168 bytes of JSON each. WalletContext.tsx:119-127 fetches /api/settings/public anyway. /api/bundles answers `public, max-age=60` with `Vary: Cookie` and no cf-cache-status (worker/routes/bundles.ts:90), so the edge never stores it.

2) None of these reads can hold the first paint, because they only start after /api/auth/me returns.
- WalletContext.tsx:172-178 waits for `authLoaded`.
- useCommunityAccess (src/pages/community/access.tsx:107-111) waits for `isLoaded`.
- In every phone run they start at or after the first paint. For example on /categories/printer-accessories the first paint is at 2336 ms and access starts at 2429 ms.
- On / the duplicate settings read starts after the largest paint in both audit runs: 2767 ms vs 2476 ms, and 3500 ms vs 3172 ms. The duplicate costs a phone user on / nothing.

3) Nothing on screen waits for their answers.
- Prices render in dinars by default. With USD chosen, `resolveDisplayRate` (src/CurrencyContext.tsx) uses the cached shop rate until settings arrive. docs/PERFORMANCE_LOG.md:666 already records "Nothing on the page blocks on /api/settings/public".
- Access only decides the BottomNav community tab.
- CategoriesExplorer.tsx:82-85 fetches /api/bundles?limit=4 alongside the other reads and only adds an optional banner. The live answer is `{"bundles":[]}` (49 bytes).

4) The 1.4–1.5 s durations come from the shared link; the requests do not cost that time. Together they are 5.9 KB on the wire (7.3 KB with bundles on /categories). At the audit's Slow-4G (200 KB/s) that is about 30–37 ms of link time, and that is the most they can take from the chunks.

5) Real-browser A/B, phone profile (360×800 DPR 3, CPU ×4, Slow-4G), cold context each run, live site. A = normal. C = settings, access and bundles held unanswered for the whole page load, which is the most any deferral could gain.
- /categories/printer-accessories, largest paint: A 5776 / 5700 / 6044 ms; C 5828 / 5164 / 6268 ms.
- On the same route, the start of the /api/catalog request (the step that gates the first image): A 4131 / 3899 / 4106 ms; C 4134 / 3895 / 3918 ms. It did not move.
- /categories, largest paint: A 5432 / 4180 ms; C 4544 / 4508 ms.
- These differences are run-to-run noise of ±500 ms or more, with no direction.
- Logs: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-shellreads/ab-pacc.log and ab-cat.log. Script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-shellreads/ab.cjs.

6) /api/bundles without edge caching, measured with curl on a reused connection: 90–220 ms, against about 66 ms for edge-cached settings and access. That is about 50–150 ms of Worker time on a request nothing waits for. It is worth fixing as hygiene (anonymousCached is already used for similar public reads), not as a display fix.

Verdict: the cost is negligible for a phone user's display. "Low" overstates it; it is cleanup, not a cause of slow pages. Seeding WalletContext from /api/home and putting /api/bundles behind anonymousCached are harmless tidy-ups.

The code facts are right, but none of these reads holds up display, and removing all three outright made no measurable difference on the live site.

What is true:
- /api/home carries a `settings` object identical to /api/settings/public: 6,451 bytes of JSON each, same keys, equal.
- WalletContext.tsx:118-127 and :172-178 fetch the settings again on every load, once /api/auth/me has resolved.
- BottomNav.tsx:171 and DashboardLayout.tsx:218 read /api/community/access.
- bundles.ts:90 sends `public, max-age=60` with no s-maxage, and curl shows no cf-cache-status. So /api/bundles is not edge-cached.

Why it is not a cause of slow display:
1. Nothing waits on these answers.
   - Storefront pages never read the wallet's `isLoaded`. Only Cart, Checkout, Wallet, OrderDetail, Product (settings) and admin screens read `settings`.
   - Prices default to IQD. A USD reader falls back to the cached rate (CurrencyContext.tsx:159-172, 273-276).
   - useCommunityAccess (pages/community/access.tsx:105-133) is used only to HIDE a community tab or tile after the page has rendered (BottomNav.tsx:162-177, ServicesGrid.tsx:74, PrinterFinder.tsx:29).
   - /api/bundles is a separate promise in CategoriesExplorer.tsx:82-85. Live it returns `{"entitled":false,"signed_in":false,"bundles":[]}` (49 bytes), and its banner renders only when the list is non-empty (line 112).
2. On /, the duplicate settings read cannot touch the LCP. live-1.log has the phone LCP at 2476 ms (the h1), while settings is only requested at 2767 ms, after the LCP.
3. The bandwidth share is tiny. In the phone trace of /categories/printer-accessories, the two reads carry 6,084 bytes out of the 172,390 bytes that load between the chunk burst (2459 ms) and the catalog fetch (4140 ms). That is 3.5%, or 29 ms at 1.6 Mbps.
4. Upper-bound A/B on the live site, my own script (scratchpad/perf/skeptic-shellreads-y/ab.cjs). Phone profile matching perf-live-audit.mjs: 360x800, DPR 3, CPU x4, Slow-4G. Cold, runs interleaved. Mode A is as served; mode H holds settings, access and bundles for the whole measured window, so it bounds any deferral from above. Medians:

| Route | Runs | LCP, A (ms) | LCP, H (ms) | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| /categories/printer-accessories | 7 + 7 | 5384 | 5412 | catalog fetch start (end of chunk window): 3925 A vs 3974 H |
| /categories | 6 + 6 | 4480 | 4548 | catalog/tree start: 3169 A vs 3099 H |
| / | 5 + 5 | 2444 | 2548 | — |

   The run-to-run spread is about ±400 ms, and removing the reads is no faster.
5. The "1.22 s cold" for /api/bundles is a fresh connection, not Worker cost. On a fresh connection curl took 0.97 s for bundles and 0.80 s for the edge-cached settings. On a reused connection, bundles (Worker) took 87-248 ms and community/access (edge HIT) took 66-98 ms. Edge caching would save about 50-150 ms on a request nothing waits for.

The proposed fix also has a downside. Community is closed live (`may_enter: false`). The bottom bar shows the community tab until the access answer arrives, then removes it. Deferring the access read with afterCriticalPaint would keep that wrong tab on screen longer and move the bar's reflow later. Deferring settings would also delay the dollar reading for a first-time USD reader. Seeding WalletContext from /api/home on / is harmless, but it only removes one 4.3 KB request that already starts after the LCP.

refuted.title: A dimmed full-screen 'loading' overlay covers the already-drawn page on every cold product-page load
reasons:
The overlay is real in the DOM, but it is never drawn on a cold load, so it hides nothing and delays nothing on screen.

1. It stays at opacity 0. In 3 cold phone runs of /product/esun-pla-plus (360x800, DPR 3, CPU x4, Slow-4G), the live `[data-app-busy="route"]` node read `style="z-index: 300; touch-action: none; opacity: 0;"`, computed opacity "0", with no running animations. Sampling it every animation frame for its whole life gave opacity 0.00 in every sample of 6 runs (11 to 29 samples each). Screenshots taken while it was mounted show no dimming, no spinner and no «جارٍ التحميل…» label. busy-p3.png shows the plain fallback screen and busy-p2.png the product page fully lit.

2. The code explains why. AppBusy renders a Motion `m.div` inside `<MotionFeatures>` (src/components/ui/AppBusy.tsx:258-289, `initial="hidden"`). MotionFeatures is a `LazyMotion` whose features come from a lazy `import('./motionFeaturesBundle')` (src/lib/motionFeatures.tsx). On a cold load nothing has loaded that bundle yet: `preloadMotionFeatures` only runs after the home page's critical paint or on the first pointer over a link (src/App.tsx:211-225). So the node renders its `hidden` state (opacity 0) and cannot animate to `shown`. The features bundle is requested only when the overlay mounts. Its request finished at 3216-3702 ms on the test script's clock, which runs about 70 ms ahead of page time. By then the route had already committed (fallback gone at 2891-3312 ms). The exit then runs from 0 to 0 and removes the node at 3136-3631 ms. That removal is the "leaves at 3.4-3.8 s" the render audit counted as a visible overlay. The audit measured DOM presence, not visibility.

3. A/B of the proposed fix shows no display gain. In 6 interleaved cold pairs, A served the live entry `index-oWU6EvxE.js` unchanged and B served it patched `!(e==="route"&&m)` -> `!(e==="route")`, so a route wait never shows the overlay. Both were served from one local copy with the same Slow-4G delay:
   - Fallback gone: A median 3085 ms, B 2966 ms.
   - Product h1: A 3386 ms, B 3338 ms.
   - LCP: A 3916 ms, B 3816 ms.
   - The per-pair differences have both signs (h1: -153 to +228 ms; LCP: -112 to +200 ms), so the gap is run-to-run noise.

The only extra request the overlay causes is `motionFeaturesBundle-5ZYeGhU5.js`, which is 117 bytes over brotli. Its dependency, `vendor-motion-DDNunUBr.js`, is already modulepreloaded on the product page.

What is real, and is an input problem rather than a display one: the invisible layer at z-index 300 swallows pointer events (AppBusy.tsx:265-269). After the product page has committed, it stays mounted for 245-332 ms (fallback gone -> node removed: 319, 332, 327, 245, 287, 293 ms) until the features bundle arrives. In one run a hit test at the header returned the overlay. The fix is to not mount the route overlay until it can actually be drawn, or to unmount it immediately when the wait ends instead of waiting for the exit animation. The proposed "booting until AppIntro reports" change would also remove this, but its stated benefit (0.6-0.9 s of dimmed spinner) does not exist.

Evidence is in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-routebusy/ (ab.mjs, ab-product.jsonl, shot.mjs, busy-p2.png, busy-p3.png). The fdm listing showed no overlay in 3 cold runs; the code path is the same, so it would also be invisible.

The finding measured whether the overlay node was in the DOM. It never checked whether anyone could see it. On the stated phone profile it is never visible, and when it does show it hides no content.

1) Why it is invisible. src/components/ui/AppBusy.tsx:255-289 draws the scrim as an `m.div` (motion/react-m) inside `<MotionFeatures>`, with `initial="hidden"`, which is opacity 0. Until the lazy LazyMotion features load, an `m` element stays at its `initial` values (src/lib/motionFeatures.tsx header). On a cold load nothing has fetched that chunk yet: it is requested only when the overlay itself mounts (motionFeaturesBundle-5ZYeGhU5.js, 117 B br; it imports vendor-motion, which the product document already modulepreloads). So the scrim mounts at opacity 0. The features then arrive about 100 ms after the route fallback has already gone. By then `visible` is false, so the exit runs from 0 to 0 and the scrim never appears.

2) My measurements. Real Chromium, cold, 360x800 DPR 3, CPU x4, Slow-4G (150 ms latency, 1.6 Mbps), 5 runs of /product/esun-pla-plus. Every animation frame I sampled the computed opacity of [data-app-busy] multiplied through its ancestors.
- In 5 of 5 runs the maximum effective opacity was 0 (17-54 samples per run). The node was in the DOM for 0.4-1.2 s (for example 2842 to 4071 ms) with inline opacity "0" the whole time.
- When the features landed vs when the route fallback left: 3633 vs 3509, 3744 vs 3662, 3622 vs 3521, 3894 vs 3789, 4445 vs 4454 ms.
- The screencast shows a plain cream canvas at 3050 ms while the scrim is in the DOM, then the undimmed skeleton at 3577 ms. No spinner and no dimming at any point.
- FCP is the skeleton itself (3564 ms against fallback removal at 3509), so nothing drawn earlier was hidden. The "header and canvas since about 2.4 s" is a blank canvas.
- A parallel A/B already in the scratchpad (skeptic-routebusy/ab-product.jsonl, where variant B patches the route overlay out of the entry) agrees: opacity was 0 in all 3 A runs. Skeleton to h1 took about 320-330 ms with the overlay and 318-577 ms without it, and LCP (3884-4152 ms vs 3696-3996 ms) is within run noise. The h1 timing comes from the product data, not from the overlay.

3) When it does show, it hides no content. I made one slower run (700 kbps, 300 ms latency, CPU x6), and only there did the scrim appear, at up to 0.98 opacity. By frame brightness it fades in at 7635 ms and is fully dim from about 7740 to 7825 ms, while the screen underneath is a blank fallback. The skeleton commits at 7764 ms, and the AppIntro mounted at the same moment so the stand-down applied. The scrim is gone by about 7900 ms. The h1 (8204 ms) and LCP (9072 ms) both arrive after it has left. That is about 0.25 s of dimming over a blank screen and then a fading skeleton, and it delays no content.

4) The listing page. On /categories/printing-materials/fdm-materials, AppIntro mounts early (2484-2799 ms). In 2 runs the scrim either never mounted or was in the DOM for 52 ms (2846 to 2898 ms) at opacity 0. Its only side effect there is pulling vendor-motion (16.9 KB br) ahead of the idle prefetch, about 85 ms of Slow-4G bandwidth.

What is real is minor and not about speed. During boot the invisible scrim still swallows taps for 0.4-1.2 s. On slow networks it can flash a roughly 0.25 s spinner that the code's own stand-down rule (the mascot is the boot loader) meant to prevent. The proposed fix (no 'route' overlay before the first commit or the intro) is harmless and fixes both. It would not make the skeleton, h1 or LCP appear any sooner, because those are gated by the Product chunk closure and the product data.

Evidence, all under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-busyoverlay/:
- probe script: probe.mjs and probe-slow.mjs
- results: results-p.jsonl, results-p2.jsonl, results-fdm.jsonl, results-slow.jsonl
- frames: frames-p-1/03050.jpg and 03577.jpg (no dimming); frames-slow-1/07737.jpg (dimmed with spinner over a blank screen) and 07904.jpg (already gone over the skeleton)

refuted.title: Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon is injected into every page inside the critical window
reasons:
The facts are right, but the cost is too small to measure. I re-measured on live with a blind A/B test, and the beacon is not a real cause of slow display.

What is true:
- Cloudflare injects `<script type="module" src="https://static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js/v4bc70e2c01a94c73b74392e4234840661791215815920" ...>` just before `</body>`. It only does this for browser-like requests: curl with `Accept: text/html` gets the tag, plain curl does not.
- The script is 10,664 B on the wire (31.7 KB raw), served with `cache-control: public, max-age=86400`. So it costs a first-time visitor about 10 KB once a day.
- It is requested at High priority at about 0.27 s, alongside the entry. Three `/cdn-cgi/rum` POSTs (~740 B each) follow after the load event.
- Nothing in the repo loads it. `worker/lib/securityPolicy.ts:34-48` and `:78-80` only allow it in the CSP so the owner's analytics keeps working.

Why it does not slow display:

1. **It does not block rendering.** A `type=module` script is deferred: it never blocks the parser or the first paint. The page is client-rendered into an empty `#root`. React's first render is scheduled as a separate task, and lazy route chunks are not in the deferred-script queue. So the beacon can only touch display by adding main-thread work or by delaying the window `load` event.

2. **It does not delay `load`.** On phone runs the beacon finished at about 0.94–1.25 s, roughly 0.8 s before the app's own entry module graph finished (about 1.9–3.3 s). The app's own module graph is still downloading when it lands, so it is never the last thing `load` waits for. That matters because the deferred home sections, idle prefetch and service-worker registration wait for `load` (`src/lib/afterCriticalPaint.ts:23`, `src/pages/Home.tsx:139`, `src/main.tsx:107-111`). The A/B shows `load` minus document end changing by only +6 to +45 ms.

3. **The main-thread cost is a third of what the finding claims.** I took a full trace of `/product/esun-pla-plus` on the phone profile (CPU ×4, Slow-4G):
   - Its 267 ms parse runs on a background script-streaming thread (`v8.parseOnBackground`), not the main thread.
   - Main-thread `FunctionCall` totals 30.6 ms across the whole 9 s trace, not 73 ms. About 10 ms of that falls before FCP, and the largest single slice is 7.4 ms.
   - Module compile is 0.5 ms.
   - The rum POSTs went out at 3.85–4.08 s and finished at 4.5–5.0 s. The LCP image requests started at 6.24 s, so they did not overlap.

4. **The blind A/B shows no significant difference.** Same phone profile as `perf-live-audit.mjs` (360×800, DPR 3, CPU ×4, 150 ms latency, 1.6 Mbps), cold context per visit, beacon allowed vs blocked with `Network.setBlockedURLs`, alternating order, 72 visits. Times are medians measured from the end of the document response:

| Route | Visits per arm | FCP change with beacon | LCP change with beacon | p (LCP) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/` | 6 | +31 ms | +31 ms | 0.51 |
| `/products` | 6 | −15 ms | −96 ms | 0.34 |
| `/product/esun-pla-plus` | 16 | +29 ms | +196 ms | 0.10 |
| `/categories/printing-materials/fdm-materials` | 10 | +0.5 ms | +175 ms | 0.27 |

   - Pooling the image-LCP routes (31 vs 32 visits) gives about +78 ms (mean), p = 0.32.
   - FCP is unchanged within noise everywhere.
   - Run-to-run spread on the same route is about 400–1,300 ms, so any real effect is well below what a phone user would notice.

5. **The proposed fix cannot be done as written.** "Load the beacon after the window load event" is not possible from code: Cloudflare injects the tag at the edge, after the Worker runs. The only choices are:
   - the owner turns Web Analytics injection off in the dashboard, or
   - the CSP stops allowing it, which kills analytics and logs a CSP violation on every page. That is what happened before the allowance was added (`securityPolicy.ts:34-48`).

   Either way it is the owner's analytics decision, not a speed fix.

Measurements are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-cfbeacon/ab-1.log`, `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-cfbeacon/ab-2.log` and `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-cfbeacon/trace-product.json`. The scripts are `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-cfbeacon/tools/ab.cjs` and `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-cfbeacon/tools/trace.cjs`.

The beacon is real, but what it costs a phone is too small to matter. I re-measured it on the live site with Playwright Chromium on the phone profile (360x800 DPR3, CPU x4, Slow-4G 150 ms / 1.6 Mbps, cold context). I ran 4 home visits with the beacon allowed and 4 with it blocked by Network.setBlockedURLs, and traced 2 of them.

What the finding gets right:
- The edge injects `<script type="module" src="https://static.cloudflareinsights.com/beacon.min.js/..." integrity crossorigin>` as the last child of `<body>` (curl of / today).
- Nothing in the repo loads it. worker/lib/securityPolicy.ts:34-48 and :78-80 only allow it in the CSP.
- It is requested at about 0.28 s at High priority, 10,664 B on the wire, finishing at 1.1-1.8 s.
- It sends 2-3 POSTs of about 750 B to /cdn-cgi/rum.

Why it does not slow display:
1. It is not render-blocking: resource timing reports renderBlockingStatus=non-blocking.
2. It cannot delay the app's start. It is a later non-async module in document order, so the entry module runs as soon as its own imports arrive. In the trace, entry evaluation starts at 2017 ms, right after vendor-react finishes at 2000 ms. The beacon had already arrived at 1385 ms.
3. It does not push back DOMContentLoaded or window load, so it does not delay src/lib/afterCriticalPaint.ts:23 (Home.tsx:139, Product.tsx:1997, App.tsx:211). In every allowed run it finished 300-800 ms before the entry graph.
4. The "~70 ms CPU" claim is mis-stated. Beacon main-thread time is 44.6 ms over the whole trace (41 ms in the first 4.2 s at x4 CPU), in slices under 10 ms, so it causes no long tasks. Only 11.1 ms falls before FCP: 0.8 ms in the DOMContentLoaded handler, plus about 10 ms at 2683-2693 ms. That second slice comes after the first frame was already painted (Paint task at 2627-2662 ms), so it does not delay the paint. Parsing happens off the main thread; compileModule takes 0.08 ms.
5. The extra handshake is to another host on its own connection, in parallel, and blocks nothing.
6. The rum POSTs start after the load event (2233 ms and later). They are about 750 B of upload, and no levonis-iq.com request after them stalled (sendStart 47-95 ms).
7. It is cached `public, max-age=86400`, so warm visits and in-app navigations pay nothing.

The only real cost is that the beacon shares bandwidth with the first-load JS on a cold visit:
- Theory: 10,664 B / 204.8 KB/s = 52 ms.
- Measured: critical JS finished 1678 ms (allowed) vs 1636 ms (blocked) after the HTML arrived, medians of n=4 each. That is a 42 ms difference.
- FCP minus HTML-arrival: medians 2266 ms allowed vs 2172 ms blocked, but runs spread by ±130 ms, so that difference is inside the noise.

In the raw FCP numbers, the slower allowed runs were caused by HTML arriving late (TTFB 0.68 s and 1.0 s), not by the beacon.

Even the 42 ms is about 2% of a 2.4-6 s LCP, and only on a first cold visit. The proposed fix of turning the injection off would also take away the owner's Web Analytics, which the securityPolicy.ts comment says the owner once lost and wanted back, for no visible gain.

A caveat on the lab: the egress proxy forces HTTP/1.1 for every origin, which inflates per-host queueing, but not for the beacon, which is on a separate host. Total traffic was about 320 page-load requests plus 3 curl requests.

Evidence is in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-cfbeacon-z/runs (home-a1..a4 and home-b1..b4, .json, plus traces for a1 and b1). Scripts are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Levonis/aa8068a2-6eee-5a26-9836-675f1c2740c2/scratchpad/perf/skeptic-cfbeacon-z/tools.

refuted.title: Product page downloads every thumbnail and colour-swatch photo together with the main photo, mostly outside the screen
reasons:
The off-screen requests are real, but they do not delay anything a phone user sees.

What is true: the live page (now built from a newer commit, Product-BRPeh8Sn.js, where the same code sits at Product.tsx:3729-3736 for colour chips and 4266-4287 for thumbnails) requests a lot of off-screen images. On /product/bambu-lab-pla-basic-filament an unthrottled 360x800 run fetched 57 images (208 KB): 6 on screen (the main photo and 5 thumbnails), plus 21 thumbnails and 30 colour-chip photos off screen (about 145 KB). The colour grid starts at y=868 on an 800px-tall screen. All 30 colours carry `hex`. The script is classify.mjs.

What is wrong: the claim that they are requested "in the same 100 ms" as the main photo and steal its bandwidth. That timestamp is `requestWillBeSent`, which is when the page asks for the image, not when it goes on the wire. queue.mjs reads the real send time (`timing.requestTime + sendStart`). The main photo (High priority) was sent first, at 3908 ms. Chrome held the Low-priority lazy images for up to 2.2 s, and the 39 off-screen ones went out between 4433 and 6332 ms. The on-screen thumbnails were raised to High and went before them.

A/B test, cold phone, CPU x4, Slow-4G, live site, same profile as the finding. "normal" is the page as it is; "fix" never requests the 39 off-screen images.
- ab2.mjs (off-screen requests aborted), 8 rounds each: main-photo download median 592 vs 589 ms, paired difference median +32 ms (range -95 to +112). Image-arrived-to-paint 118 vs 115 ms. On-screen thumbnails done 5246 vs 5198 ms.
- ab.mjs (off-screen requests held open), 8 rounds each: download 578 vs 650 ms (the fix was not faster). LCP 5044 vs 5272 ms.
- ab3.mjs, 3 rounds each: paired download median -15 ms.
- The LCP spread between runs (4.3 to 8.2 s) comes from when the main-photo request started. That is fixed before any thumbnail exists, so it is not contention.
- The window `load` event fires at about 2.5 s, before any product image is requested. So these images do not hold `load`, and `afterCriticalPaint` only waits for on-screen images. The only gated work is the logged-in quick-buy prefetch. Nothing visible waits for the 1.9 s network tail (last image done 7069 vs 5198 ms).

Caveat: this sandbox's proxy makes Chromium use HTTP/1.1 (`nextHopProtocol` is http/1.1), and so did the finding's trace. Real phones use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, where all requests go out at once. There, Chrome's stream priorities put the main photo ahead of every Low image. The main photo is also an edge cache hit (cf-cache-status HIT, x-variant-source edge) and is requested about 110 ms earlier. So Cloudflare should send it first. I could not measure HTTP/2 from here; if Cloudflare ignored priorities, the worst case would be about +0.5 s.

The proposed −150 to −250 ms LCP is not supported. Drawing chips from `hex` would also change the design the owner chose (spool photos), only to save data.

The facts in the finding are correct, but the cause it claims does not happen. Nothing off-screen slows down what the phone shows.

What is true: on /product/bambu-lab-pla-basic-filament all 30 colours carry `hex` (I checked the live /api/products JSON, 30 of 30). Each colour chip still draws its bound photo through SafeImage with sizes="36px" (src/pages/Product.tsx:3577-3584). Every gallery thumb is a lazy SafeImage with sizes="64px" (4125-4133). SafeImage marks every non-eager picture loading="lazy" and fetchPriority="auto" (src/components/ui/SafeImage.tsx:162-173). Chrome's margin fetches about 15 strip thumbs and all 30 swatches. The swatch tops are 868-1854 px, below the fold. A cold phone visit loads 45 images / 170 KB, and about 102 KB of that is off-screen.

Why the claim fails:

1. The finding's own trace contradicts it (perf/product/runs/bambu-lab-pla-basic-filament-b.json).
   - The main photo starts at 3490 ms, gets its first byte at 3720 and finishes at 4031.
   - The other images take a median of 1431 ms to their first byte.
   - Only 3 images get any bytes before the main photo finishes, and all 3 are first-screen thumbs: the main photo's own w=320 copy, 2ce369 and d5ef1a.
   - No off-screen thumb or swatch receives a single byte before the main photo is done.
   - p1s trace: the only overlap is the main photo's own w=320 thumb.
   - So nothing off-screen shares the 1.6 Mbps link with the LCP photo. The off-screen requests start about 95 ms after it, at Low priority (the main photo is High), and arrive after it.

2. Nothing visible waits for them.
   - The load event fires at about 0.9 s, before the app has asked for any image.
   - afterCriticalPaint on this page only gates the quick-buy check for signed-in users (Product.tsx:1997), and it waits only for images on screen.
   - "The page settles seconds earlier" refers to pictures off the screen.

3. My own A/B on the live site (perf/skeptic-swatchlazy/ab.mjs, logs pla2.log and pla3.log).
   - Setup: 360x800 DPR 3, CPU x4, 150 ms latency, 1.6 Mbps. App assets were served from memory so the comparison isolates images.
   - The "fix" arm blocks at the network layer (Network.setBlockedURLs) every /files/ URL that is not on the first screen: 51 URLs, leaving the main photo and 5 thumbs. That is the best case for the proposed fix.
   - 16 alternating runs per arm, medians, normal vs fix:

   | Measure (ms) | normal | fix |
   |---|---|---|
   | LCP minus main-photo request start | 674.5 | 690.5 |
   | All first-screen images done, minus main-photo start | 866 | 909.5 |
   | Main-photo body | 258 | 232 |
   | Paint after the main photo arrives | 118 | 106.5 |
   | FCP | 1294 | 1324 |
   | Image bytes | 170 KB | 68 KB |

   - Blocking the off-screen images saves bytes, not display time.
   - An earlier skeptic run (perf/skeptic-thumbstrip-c/ab-slow4g.log, n=5 per arm) found the same: LCP 2480 vs 2492 ms.

4. The proposed fix has a cost of its own.
   - The colours sit below the fold, and Chrome's margin is what makes them ready by the time a user scrolls there.
   - With a tight IntersectionObserver margin, each chip would appear only after its own server wait, which is 300-1400 ms on this link.
   - Drawing chips from hex instead changes how they look (photos of spools), which is the owner's design choice, not a speed fix.

What is left is data, not display: about 102 KB per visit on many-colour filaments (170 to 68 KB) and about 38 KB on printers. Each swatch's w=160 copy is a second download of a photo whose w=320 copy the thumbnail strip also loads. That is worth a low-priority cleanup, for example letting chips reuse the w=320 copy or loading the strip beyond the visible thumbs later. It is not a cause of slow display.
